# SQ3 robustness experiment — first run, 2026-08-13

**All portfolios are SYNTHETIC**, generated by `robustness.py` and labelled as such.
108 scenario cells × 100 draws = 10,800 portfolios, seed 42, reproducible with:

```bash
python3 -m optimiser.robustness
```

Results: `robustness_results_2026-08-13.csv`. Solver: exact enumeration of the
Chapter 3 formulation (equations 3.3 to 3.6), cross-checked against the Gurobi model
in `tests/test_robustness.py` (18 tests pass, including the cross-check).

## Design

| Axis | Values | Grounding |
|---|---|---|
| Arrival timing (days left at planning) | early 30–60, typical 5–50, late −30–25 | typical reflects the tracker's median week of pre-queue delay; late reflects its long tail |
| Aseptic share | 0.4, 0.6, 0.8 | centred on the trust's own 60% (Q6) |
| Prescription share | 0.2, 0.4 | no trust figure exists, so varied rather than assumed |
| Scores and threshold | all-high floor 20; spread floor 20; spread floor 30 | all-high mirrors today: every scored study is in the top band |
| Duration regime | illustrative 25/36/45; measured-like 95 flat | 95 is the pooled tracker median |

Comparator: arrival order (commit the longest-waiting up to the limit of 3).
**This comparator flatters the model** — LTHTR answer Q4-2 records that real practice
already accelerates studies judged important — so any advantage is an upper bound.

## Findings

**1. The rule never does worse on the on-time count, but that is by construction.**
The model attains the maximum achievable P1, so losses are structurally impossible.
The reportable finding is how often it does *better* than arrival order, not that it
never does worse.

**2. Where trials are rescueable, it beats arrival order in roughly four draws in ten.**
Across illustrative-duration cells with early or typical timing: 1,548 wins in 3,600
draws (43%; 52% in typical timing alone). Wins survive every aseptic share, both
prescription shares and all three score scenarios, so the advantage is robust to the
mix and the threshold. A tighter threshold (floor 30) shrinks the eligible queue and
with it the room to differ: wins fall to 9% of those cells' draws.

**3. With measured durations, the advantage vanishes entirely — and the model
reproduces arrival order.** At 95-day durations nothing is rescueable, P1 is zero for
every plan, and minimising weighted lateness reduces to committing the longest-waiting
trials, which is exactly what the service does today. Mean P2 difference: 0.0 weighted
days across all 5,400 such draws. This is worth stating in Chapter 5: **on current
durations the model validates current practice rather than beating it**, and its value
appears only as the service recovers (or durations shorten) enough for some trials to
be rescueable.

**4. The on-time gain has a price in weighted days.** In 24 of 108 cells the model's
weighted lateness is *worse* than arrival order's (worst cell: −20.6 weighted days,
typical timing, all-high scores, illustrative durations). This is the lexicographic
ordering working as designed: P1 buys rescues first and pays for them in P2. It is the
same price-of-rescue trade the frontier analysis in
`Model/Merged_Model_Specification_EN.md` reports, reproduced independently here.

## Caveats

- Synthetic durations, synthetic arrivals; the 16–20 real cases recalibrate both.
- The comparator understates current practice (Q4-2), so win rates are upper bounds.
- Timing "late" cells: nothing is rescueable at any plan size, so all draws tie.
- Claim weights use notified-based waiting in the real code but queue-entry waiting
  here, matching the August correction the code has not yet received.

## Where this lands in the dissertation

Chapter 4 describes the generator and this design. Chapter 5 reports findings 2–4
against SQ3. Chapter 6 carries finding 3's implication: the model's headline value is
conditional on durations, which are the chapter's first-listed unmeasured assumption.

# Second run, 2026-08-26 — recalibrated after the August return

**Rerun under the recompute-report calibration**, replacing `illustrative` and
`measured95`, both retired. Same seed (42), grid, comparator and draw count, so the
two CSVs differ only in the duration axis. 270 cells x 100 draws = 27,000 portfolios.
Results: `robustness_results_2026-08-26.csv`, produced by
`Experiments/run_robustness_real_2026-08-26.py`.

| Regime | Durations (Routine / Presc / AsepOnly / Both) | Source |
|---|---|---|
| calibrated ±20% | 142 / 102 / 102 / 79, at 0.8x, 1.0x, 1.2x | recompute §3, real-return medians |
| standards | 50 / 30 / 72 / 60 | recompute §12, floor-top work standards |
| service62 | 62 flat | `SERVICE_P25_CLOCK` |

## Findings

**1. At current performance the on-time objective is dead everywhere.** All three
calibrated regimes: 0 wins in 16,200 draws — even at 0.8x, every pathway duration
(63 to 114 days) exceeds the 52-day setup ceiling, so no trial is ever rescueable and
the model can only tie arrival order. `service62` is dead for the same reason: the
achievable pooled p25 of 62 still exceeds 52. This is section 9's structural finding
reproduced by simulation.

**2. Only the standards regime keeps the on-time objective alive: 19% wins overall,
40% in early timing, 0% in late.** Wins require both demonstrated-floor performance
AND early arrival — echoing the preparation finding from the opposite direction.
Win rate falls monotonically with aseptic share (24.6% at 0.4, 12.9% at 0.8), because
only Routine (50) and Prescription-only (30) clear the 52-day ceiling; Both (60) and
Aseptic-only (72) miss it even at their floors.

**3. The P1 gain is bought with P2 lateness, and the price is visible.** In standards
cells with wins, mean P2 saving is **−7.0 weighted days** (worst cell −24.6): the model
commits rescueable trials ahead of longest-waiting ones, accepting extra weighted
lateness on the deferred to buy on-time completions. This is the lexicographic
hierarchy working as designed — P1 is senior — but Chapter 5 must report the price,
not just the wins. Cells without wins: P2 saving 0.0, exact ties throughout.

**4. Zero losses in 27,000 draws**, as before, and as before this is by construction —
the reportable number is the win rate, not the absence of losses.

## Carried limitation

`SynthTrial` draws trials already queued: the sweep exercises neither equation (4.1)
nor the preparation lead (`prep_lead_days`, added 26 August). The standards-regime
result therefore *understates* what preparation could add — trials that would be
rescueable with a lead are generated without one. Extending the generator with a
hand-over distribution remains the Chapter 6 next step.

## Third run, 2026-08-29: value-score axis removed

The Prioritisation Tool left the model on 28 August (Chapter 3 §3.3), taking the eligibility
threshold with it. The sweep's `scores` axis was therefore simulating a gate the model no longer
has in two of its three levels, so `SCORES`, `Scenario.scores` and `SynthTrial.value` were
removed from `robustness.py` and the sweep rerun.

Grid: 3 timings x 3 aseptic shares x 2 prescription shares x 5 duration regimes = 90 cells,
100 draws each, 9,000 in total, seed 42. Runner `Experiments/run_robustness_real_2026-08-29.py`,
output `robustness_results_2026-08-29.csv`. 68 tests pass.

| Regime | Wins | Draws | Win rate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| calibrated-20pct | 0 | 1,800 | 0% |
| calibrated | 0 | 1,800 | 0% |
| calibrated+20pct | 0 | 1,800 | 0% |
| **standards (floors)** | **640** | **1,800** | **35.6%** |
| service62 | 0 | 1,800 | 0% |

Losses 0 across all 9,000 draws, as in both earlier runs and for the same by-construction reason.
Cost per win 24.3 weighted days (summed P2 saving -15,580 over the 18 floors cells / 640 wins).

Within the floors regime: early arrival 75.0%, typical 31.7%, late 0.0%; aseptic share 0.4 gives
44.8%, 0.6 gives 37.5%, 0.8 gives 24.3%.

**Why the headline moved from 19% to 36%.** Filtering the 26 August CSV to its `allhigh-floor20`
cells alone, the condition in which the gate excludes nobody, gives 664 of 1,800 = 36.9%. The old
19% was an average over two gate settings the model does not have. The finding is unchanged; only
the denominator was wrong.
